lesson.title: How machines learn
lesson.subtitle: Five steps from examples to a working model

video.title: How machines learn
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Okafor — science teacher, Nigeria (main character)
Ms Amina Bello — teacher at the same school (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice, talking to the student (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor in the staff room, phone in hand, showing the class WhatsApp group: a forwarded message with a bright banner, ‘Free data for every student, click here!’, the same one as last week further up. He sighs, then looks up with an idea.
scenes.animation: The message bubble slides up with a small bounce; the older copy above it highlights. Push-in on his raised eyebrows.
scenes.narration: Every week, someone forwards the same scam to our class group: “Free data for every student, click here!” What if we taught a computer to catch these for us?

scenes.visual: Paper-grey card. The Darsi mark pops in, then the course name, the lesson title and the AI track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark scales in with a small overshoot (≤ 200 ms); title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: how machines learn, in five steps you could follow yourself.

scenes.visual: Students around a desk with a shared phone and a notebook. Message cards (lines only, names blurred out) pile up; twenty slide into a box marked ‘later’. Hands clip a tag on every card, including the twenty in the box: a shield (safe) or a warning triangle (scam).
scenes.animation: Cards fly into a pile; the box closes on twenty; tags clip on, 150 ms each.
scenes.narration: Step one: collect examples. Your class gathers a hundred messages, takes out names and numbers, and keeps twenty aside for later. Step two: label them. Each message gets a tag: safe, or scam. Those labels are the right answers.

scenes.visual: The two labelled piles feed into a turning cog. Words light up again and again on the scam cards: ‘free’, ‘click’, ‘urgent’; on the safe cards: ‘homework’, ‘match’, ‘meeting’. A small box with a sparkle drops out: the model.
scenes.animation: The cog turns; repeated words pulse once each; the model box drops out with a bounce.
scenes.narration: Step three: train. The computer searches the labelled messages for patterns. Scams often say “free”, “click” or “urgent”. Safe ones talk about homework, matches and meetings. What it learns is kept as numbers, and that’s the model.

scenes.visual: The ‘later’ box opens. The twenty cards go to the model one at a time; it tags each, and the class’s real tag appears beside it. A tally reads 17 ticks and 3 crosses.
scenes.animation: Cards slide in one by one; check and cross badges pop (150 ms); a loop arrow points back to the cog.
scenes.on_screen_text: Test on messages it never saw
scenes.narration: Step four: test. Give the model the twenty messages you kept aside, which it has never seen. It guesses each one, and you compare with your labels. Seventeen out of twenty right? Not bad. Too many wrong? Collect more examples and train again.

scenes.visual: Clean card with the AI chip. Five steps joined by arrows: collect, label, train, test, use. The last one is filled with the AI track colour.
scenes.animation: Steps appear one by one, 300 ms apart, arrows drawing between them.
scenes.narration: That’s machine learning: the computer finds patterns in labelled examples, instead of a person writing every rule. Collect, label, train, test. Then step five: use it to sort new messages.

scenes.visual: Two students revising at a kitchen table by lamplight. One recites last year’s paper word for word; the other works through the method in a notebook. In the exam hall, a new question appears: the first student freezes, the second starts writing.
scenes.animation: Split screen; the new exam question flips in; a small check pops beside the second student.
scenes.narration: It’s like revising for exams. If you memorise last year’s paper, you’ll ace that paper. But the real exam has new questions. Only new questions show whether you learned the method.

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor holds up a score card: 20/20, with a small note, ‘training messages’. Two answer cards drop in beside him.
scenes.animation: Mr Okafor slides in; answer cards drop with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! Our model scored twenty out of twenty on the messages it trained on. Is it ready to use?

scenes.visual: The ‘Not yet’ card gets a check badge. The 20/20 score card turns over to show the same twenty messages it trained on, then the ‘later’ box opens beside it.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops (150 ms); the score card flips.
scenes.narration: Not yet. It may simply have memorised those messages, like memorising a past paper. Only messages it has never seen show whether it learned the patterns.

scenes.visual: The ‘safe’ pile is all formal teacher messages; a friend’s message full of slang and emojis gets a wrong warning tag. Then a scam in another language slides past an English-only pile. New, varied cards join both piles.
scenes.animation: The wrong tag wobbles; the scam slips by; new cards fan in.
scenes.narration: Variety matters as much as numbers. Say every safe message you collected came from teachers. Then a friend’s message full of slang might look like a scam. And if every scam was in English, a scam in another language may slip through. More examples help, and more varied ones help most.

scenes.visual: The Darsi ‘Teach the machine’ lab on a phone: two groups, ‘Safe message’ and ‘Phishing’, each with two example messages and an ‘Add example’ button. In the test box, ‘Click now to keep your account’; the guess ‘Phishing’ appears with a confidence bar.
scenes.animation: A new example drops into a group (150 ms); the confidence bar fills left to right in 1 s.
scenes.narration: In the lab, you teach the machine yourself. Two groups, safe message and phishing, start with two examples each. Add your own, then test a new message, like “Click now to keep your account”. It shows its guess, and how confident it is.

scenes.visual: Ms Amina holds up a phone with a message: ‘Congratulations! You have won a full scholarship. Send your details today.’ Two answer cards appear beside her.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. A scam filter learned only from messages promising free data. Then a fake scholarship offer arrives. What’s most likely?

scenes.visual: The ‘It might miss it’ card gets the check badge, then three summary lines and the takeaway bar.
scenes.animation: Points arrive one by one, 250 ms apart.
scenes.narration: It might miss it: a model only knows the kinds of examples it was shown. Remember the five steps: collect, label, train, test, use. Always test on examples it has never seen. And more varied examples make a better model.

scenes.visual: Two siblings at home with a sheet of paper: shapes with a dot inside on one side, shapes without on the other. One points to a new shape and guesses. Mr Okafor smiles beside them. End card: Darsi mark.
scenes.animation: Shapes draw themselves one by one; a new shape appears and gets a guess; end card fades in.
scenes.narration: Try it yourself: play “Be the machine” with a friend or someone at home. Draw shapes that follow a secret pattern, say, all with a dot inside, and shapes that don’t. Let them work out the pattern. Then test them with new shapes.

checkpoints.prompt: Our model scored 20 out of 20 on the messages it trained on. Is it ready to use?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — it may have memorised its training messages. Only messages it has never seen show whether it learned the patterns.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a perfect score on its own training messages can mean it just memorised them. Test it on messages it has never seen.

checkpoints.prompt: A scam filter learned only from messages promising free data. A fake scholarship offer arrives. What’s most likely?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — it only knows the kinds of scams it was shown. More varied examples would help.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a scholarship scam looks different from the free-data scams it learned. It might miss it, so it needs more varied examples.
